summary: Specifies MPLS Traffic Engineering Soft Preemption, a set of protocol changes that reduce or eliminate traffic disruption when a label switched path is preempted. The old path stays up while a new one is set up. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: If someone needs your seat, you can let them have it after you have found another one, not before. Soft preemption works that way for network paths so data keeps flowing during the switch.

questions: how to avoid traffic disruption when lsps are preempted
what is the soft preemption desired flag
what is the default soft preemption timer
subtitle: How MPLS traffic engineering can warn a path that it is being bumped, so traffic moves over without being dropped.

tldr.problem: In MPLS RSVP-TE, preemption normally tears down the preempted path at once, so its traffic is likely discarded even when the link could carry it.
tldr.mechanism: A preempting node zeroes its bandwidth accounting for the path and sends a PathErr with Error Code 34 and value 1, so the head-end can reroute make-before-break. A soft preemption timer guards against open-ended under-provisioning.
tldr.outcome: Traffic need not be needlessly black-holed by mere reservation contention. The cost is brief under-provisioning of reservations while the path is rerouted.

today: RFC 5712 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the reroute error code in RFC 5710.

sections.title: Hard Preemption and the Goal
sections.content:
In an MPLS RSVP-TE network (RFC 3209), hard preemption is the default. A higher-priority path displaces a lower-priority one, and the displaced Traffic Engineering Label Switched Path (TE LSP) is torn down before it is re-established. It is not handled make-before-break, and it can disrupt a potentially large number of TE LSPs.

Without an alternative, operators either accept this or give up features, for example by using only one preemption priority. RFC 5712 adds signaling that warns the ingress router (the head-end) of a pending preemption, so it can reroute the tunnel without disruption while the preempting node is temporarily under-provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: Hard preemption is like being told to leave your seat right now. This RFC lets you be told early, so you can find another seat first.

sections.title: Why Hard Preemption Hurts
sections.content:
Hard preemption immediately tears down LSPs and disregards the traffic in transit. That nearly guarantees preempted traffic is discarded, if only briefly, until the RSVP Path Error message reaches the ingress router and a new data path is built.

Preemption can be triggered by reservation contention alone, and reservations may not reflect actual data-plane contention. The result is that lower-priority traffic can be discarded even when enough bandwidth exists for both paths. The RFC adds that in a Diffserv-enabled network one need not rely exclusively on preemption to protect the most valued traffic, since marking and queuing should already serve that purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Kicking someone out before checking whether there is room for both of you wastes a lot of good seats.

sections.title: RSVP Extensions
sections.content:
Two small protocol additions carry the feature.

First, a new flag in the SESSION-ATTRIBUTE object (for C-Type 1 and 7), Soft Preemption Desired, with value 0x40. A head-end sets it to ask that its LSP be soft preempted rather than hard preempted, when soft preemption is available.

Second, a new error value under the reroute error code defined in RFC 5710. When it soft preempts, the preempting node MUST send a PathErr with Error Code 34 ("Reroute") and value 1 ("Reroute Request Soft Preemption").
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel raises a little flag saying "please warn me first", and the warning is a special note sent back to its owner.

sections.title: The Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC uses a six-router network. Two tunnels, LSP1 (R0-R1-R5, priority 0) and LSP2 (R2-R1-R4, priority 7), each reserve 155 Mbit/s and both set the Soft Preemption Desired bit. The R1-R4 link has 155 Mbit/s reservable.

When circuit R1-R5 fails, R1 notifies the head-end of LSP1, R0, which re-signals LSP1 along R0-R1-R4-R5. That cannot fit beside LSP2 on R1-R4, so LSP2 is soft preempted at R1 because it has the numerically higher priority value.

Instead of a PathTear for LSP2, R1 zeroes its local bandwidth accounting for LSP2 and sends a PathErr with "Reroute" and "Reroute Request Soft Preemption". Head-end R2 may update its view of the network, computes a new path, reroutes make-before-break, and then the old path is torn down.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road closes and the cars from one route need the space, the car already there is asked to move over after a new lane is ready, not pushed off the road.

sections.title: What the Preempting Router Does
sections.content:
The preempting node zeroes its local bandwidth accounting for the preempted TE LSP and MUST immediately send the soft-preemption PathErr toward the head-end for each one. Messages for LSPs with the same head-end may be bundled. When RSVP MESSAGE-ID extensions (RFC 2961) are in use, the message SHOULD be sent reliably.

A local soft preemption timer MUST start on soft preemption, so under-provisioning does not last forever. If it expires, the node SHOULD send a PathTear and either a ResvTear or a PathErr with the Path_State_Removed flag. If a refresh arrives before expiry, the node MUST keep refreshing the LSP.

For choosing victims, the node SHOULD first try LSPs with the Soft Preemption Desired bit cleared. Which LSPs to preempt is a local decision, and the RFC points to RFC 4829 for algorithms. A node MAY also hard preempt, even an LSP that asked for soft preemption, under circumstances such as unacceptable link congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The router tells the owner to move, sets a stopwatch, and if the owner takes too long, it finally removes the path.

sections.title: What the Head-End Does
sections.content:
On receiving the soft-preemption PathErr, the head-end MAY first update its working copy of the traffic engineering database before computing a new path, for example with CSPF. With Diffserv and MPLS-TE together, the notice may imply that available bandwidth at that priority and numerically greater priorities is exhausted on that interface, and the head-end MAY reduce or zero it until a fresh IGP update arrives.

It then reroutes the LSP with the non-traffic-disruptive make-before-break procedure. How long it avoids the interface named in the PathErr is a local decision. The RFC concludes that no traffic will be needlessly black-holed due to mere reservation contention; any loss would come from actual congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The owner builds the new route first, moves over, and only then closes the old one.

sections.title: Interoperability, Timer and Management
sections.content:
Backward compatibility should hold if implementations followed RFC 3209. The soft preemption timer SHOULD be configurable, and a default of 30 seconds is RECOMMENDED. Configuring it to 0 is RECOMMENDED to make an implementation use hard preemption. The RFC says soft preemption is designed for MPLS RSVP-TE IP networks and may not translate to some GMPLS technologies.

For management, the preempting node and the ingress SHOULD keep accounting of which LSPs and how much capacity are under-provisioned, such as bandwidth per priority per interface, and the list of LSPs in preemption-pending status.
sections.plainLanguage: The stopwatch usually runs for thirty seconds, and setting it to zero turns the gentle method off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security issues, and the considerations of RSVP-TE in RFC 3209 still apply. It notes that temporary link under-provisioning is a less serious condition than false hard preemption, but operators should be aware of the risk if soft preemption is subverted and should apply relevant MPLS control-plane security techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster could fake the warnings, the roads could get crowded, so the control messages need protecting.
